title: The Accountability Gap
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Mulder's thesis is uncomfortable on purpose: most leaders who say they want ownership actually want everyone else to take ownership. Most leadership problems are not personality problems, they are accountability problems, and the hardest part is that accountability has to start with the leader before it can be expected of anyone else. She uses her own years of avoidance as the worked example. She could feel when something in the business was off (missed deadlines, quiet resistance, pushback from team members who did not want standards to shift, work getting done but not at the level she knew they needed), and she could articulate the vision, say the standards out loud, and rally the team around the direction. She just would not enforce any of it. Her honesty about why is the part worth sitting with. She did not enforce because she did not want to feel the discomfort of disappointing a team member she admired, did not want to be seen as difficult, did not want someone talented to leave, did not want to disrupt the fake harmony they were all pretending was real. So she let things slide, especially with the team members who quietly intimidated her, and the culture followed her lead. When the leader avoids accountability the team avoids accountability. When the leader softens the standard the team softens the effort. When the leader hesitates the team slows down. The reframe she lands on is the practical move: accountability is not aggression or harshness, it is clarity. It is the truth about what the goal actually requires. Avoiding accountability is not kindness, it is unclear leadership, and unclear leadership is expensive in money, trust, time, and self-respect. People do not lose trust when a standard is enforced. They lose trust when the bar moves based on the leader's mood, fear, or the loudest personality in the room. Her closing question is worth a leader asking honestly: where am I avoiding accountability because I do not want to feel the friction? That answer, she argues, shows you both your next level and what your team has been waiting for.

quotes: There’s a pattern I see in almost every founder, every operator, every team I’ve ever coached and definitely in myself: We say we want ownership. But what we really mean is: “I want everyone else to take ownership.” Not many leaders want to look at the uncomfortable part; the part where accountability has to start with them.

I would talk about the vision. I would say the standards out loud. I would try to rally everyone around “where we were going.” But then… I wouldn’t enforce it. Not because I didn’t care. But because I didn’t want to feel the discomfort.

I didn’t want to disappoint a team member I admired. I didn’t want to be seen as difficult. I didn’t want someone talented to leave because they didn’t want to be held to a higher bar. I didn’t want to disrupt the fake harmony we were all pretending was real.
When the leader avoids accountability, the team avoids accountability. When the leader softens the standard, the team softens the effort. When the leader hesitates, the team slows down.

Accountability isn’t about aggression. It’s not about being harsh or rigid. It’s not about perfection. Accountability is clarity. It’s alignment. It’s telling the truth about what’s actually required to reach the goal.
Avoiding accountability doesn’t make you kind. It makes you unclear. And unclear leadership is expensive. It costs money. It costs trust. It costs time. It costs respect… especially self-respect.

People don’t lose trust when you enforce a standard. They lose trust when you waffle. When you say one thing and tolerate another. When the bar moves based on your mood, your fear, or the loudest personality in the room.

If something feels “off” in your leadership right now, ask yourself the question I wish I had asked sooner: Where am I avoiding accountability because I don’t want to feel the friction? That answer will show you exactly where your next level is.” Archived from Summer Mulder on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
